e.meaning: soft goat wool named for Kashmir
e.etymology: From cashmere, the soft goat wool, an old English spelling of Kashmir, the Himalayan region where it was produced. It is used as a luxury name alongside Cash.
A pet form of Henrietta, the feminine of Henry, from Germanic words for home and ruler. In Yiddish-speaking families Henny is a pet form of Hannah.
namesakes: Henny Youngman (comedian known for Take my wife, please)

assoc.t: Henny Penny, the hen who thinks the sky is falling

e.note: Henny is common slang for Hennessy cognac.

e.etymology: A spelling of Saylor, a surname from Old French sailleor, a dancer or acrobat. Most people now hear it as the English word sailor.
A modern compound of May and the -leigh spelling of Lee, in the family of Kayleigh and Hayleigh.
A respelling of Oakley, an English surname and place name from Old English ac, oak, and leah, clearing or meadow.
A French form of a Germanic name built on haim, home, and ric, ruler, a cousin of Henry and Emery. Saint Emeric was an 11th-century Hungarian prince, known in Hungarian as Imre.
Anglicized from Welsh Gwladus, of uncertain origin, perhaps connected with gwlad, country. Saint Gwladys was a Welsh queen of about 500 AD; the name was a US favorite around 1900.
namesakes: Gladys Knight (soul singer of Midnight Train to Georgia)

e.etymology: An English surname from a place name ending in Old English land; the first part is read as either hare or grey. Harlan is the commoner form.
namesakes: Harland Sanders (Colonel Sanders, founder of KFC)

e.etymology: The Spanish and Italian spelling of Chloe, from Greek khloe, the young green growth of spring. It was a title of the goddess Demeter and is the name of a woman mentioned by Saint Paul.

assoc.t: Cloe, one of the Bratz dolls

e.etymology: The Dutch form of William, from Germanic wil, will or desire, and helm, helmet or protection. It is a royal name in the Netherlands, borne by King Willem-Alexander.
A modern name read either as a feminine of Irish Cian, ancient, or as a spelling of Kiana and Sianna.

e.meaning: from McKinley, son of the fair warrior
e.etymology: A respelling of Kinley, a surname shortened from McKinley, Gaelic Mac Fhionnlaigh, son of Fionnlagh, a name meaning fair warrior.
A form of Damian, from Greek Damianos, usually tied to damazein, to tame. Hermann Hesse's 1919 novel Demian made this spelling familiar.
Two Arabic names share this English spelling: one meaning blessings or bounties, a word from the Quran given to girls, and one meaning loftiness or excellence, given to boys.
A pet form of Elizabeth, from Hebrew Elisheva, my God is an oath; also read as Lily plus Beth. Lilibet was the childhood nickname of Queen Elizabeth II.

assoc.t: Lilibet, Queen Elizabeth II's nickname and Harry's daughter

e.etymology: From Sonora, the state in northwestern Mexico that gives its name to the Sonoran Desert. The place name's origin is uncertain; it also matches Spanish sonora, sonorous.

assoc.t: Sonora, Mexican state, and the Sonoran Desert

e.etymology: Several names share this spelling: Portuguese Rui, long linked to Rodrigo; Chinese Rui, written with characters such as those for auspicious or wise; and a Japanese name written with various kanji.
A modern American name that blends the sounds of Zamir, Jahmir and Amir.
From Arabic jud, generosity or open-handedness, used for both boys and girls. Joud is the French-style spelling common in Syria and Lebanon.
Taken from Keyshia Ka'oir, the Jamaican-born entrepreneur and wife of rapper Gucci Mane, who uses Ka'oir as the name of her cosmetics and fitness brands.

assoc.t: Keyshia Ka'oir, entrepreneur married to Gucci Mane

e.etymology: A less common spelling of Stephanie, the French feminine of Stephen, from Greek stephanos, crown or garland.
From Russian Vanya, a pet form of Ivan, the Russian John, from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. In Portuguese, Spanish and Italian it became a girls' name.
A spelling of Arabic Raniya, from rana, to gaze, written in the -iyah style of Aniyah and Saniyah. Rania is the more familiar form.
From Sanskrit Keshava, one of the names of Krishna and Vishnu, usually explained as the one with long or beautiful hair, from kesha, hair.
A medieval Norman French name, a diminutive of Germanic Avila, of uncertain meaning, and the source of the surname and later first name Evelyn. In French aveline is also a word for hazelnut.

assoc.t: Aveline, heroines in Assassin's Creed and Dragon Age

e.etymology: A modern American name in the Taliyah and Alayah family, built on the -ayah ending.
A respelling of Kayden, part of the Aiden, Jayden and Brayden family that swept the US in the 2000s.
From Hebrew li, to me, and El, God: my God, or God is mine. Lielle is a feminine-looking spelling of Liel, a modern Israeli name.
The English word baby. In US records it mostly marks children not yet named when the birth was registered, though it is a real given name in the Philippines and in Kerala, India.

assoc.t: baby, the everyday word and term of endearment
Baby, Jennifer Grey's character in Dirty Dancing
Baby, the getaway driver of Baby Driver

e.note: In US birth data this is mostly a placeholder for newborns not yet named, and it is an everyday word.

e.etymology: An American coinage of the 2000s that joins the Ja- of Jane and Janae to the -iyah ending of Aaliyah. Janiyah is the commoner spelling.
A respelling of Braxton, an English surname from a place name ending in Old English tun, settlement.

assoc.t: Braxton Hicks, the practice contractions of pregnancy

e.etymology: From Arabic amin, trustworthy or faithful. Al-Amin, the trustworthy one, was a title of the Prophet Muhammad.
e.note: Ameen is also how many Muslims write amen, a separate Arabic word with a similar sound.
